client: I've been really struggling lately trying to keep everything together while my partner is away on a work trip. therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — holding down a demanding job and being the sole parent at home, day after day, with no real break in sight. I also notice that even as you're reaching out, there's a part of you that's already bracing for disappointment, like you're protecting yourself from hoping this could help. therapist: That protective instinct makes so much sense — keeping hope at arm's length feels safer than risking another disappointment when you're already running on fumes. client: There was this one time a few months ago when I finally broke down and asked my neighbor to watch the kids for an hour so I could just breathe, and she said yes without any hesitation. It did help in that moment, but then I felt so guilty afterward, like I should be able to handle it all myself without needing to lean on someone else. So even when support works out, I end up punishing myself for needing it in the first place.
therapist: It's really telling that even in a moment that *worked* — where you asked for help and it was freely given — your mind turned it into evidence that you'd somehow failed. I'm curious about that belief that you should be able to handle everything yourself: where do you think that rule came from, and do you think you'd apply that same harsh standard to a close friend in your exact situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, no, I would never tell a friend in my situation that she was failing for asking for help — I'd probably be the first one showing up at her door with dinner. I think the rule comes from watching my mom do everything alone without ever complaining, so somewhere along the way I internalized that needing help means you're weak or not cut out for it. But even knowing that intellectually doesn't make the guilt go away when I'm actually in the moment.
therapist: You just made a really important connection — that the rule wasn't really yours to begin with, it was your mom's way of surviving, and you absorbed it as a child trying to make sense of her strength. It's one thing to understand that intellectually, but it sounds like in those real moments of need, that little girl who learned "don't ask, just cope" takes over before your wiser self can step in. I'm wondering, what do you think it would take to start treating yourself with even a fraction of the compassion you'd so naturally show that friend at her door?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
